rv.q: Overall, it's an ambitious, carefully orchestrated work that raises the bar on technological innovation.
The Broadway production of "Ghost" is a lumbering megatuner with little to offer beyond a limitless array of dazzling effects.
The songs are forgettable, the dialogue is clunky, and the special effects, while impressive, can't make up for the show's fundamental dramatic weaknesses.
The music and lyrics by Dave Stewart (the Eurythmics) and Glenn Ballard are bland and derivative.

Turns out plenty in this leaden stage musicalization of the supernatural romantic thriller, a flavorless hash that is unrelentingly loud, vulgar and stunningly tone-deaf to the ways in which the world has changed since that era of sweet young yuppie innocence.
It is just as flavorless and lacking in dramatic vitality as many that have come before.
There is so much wrong with "Ghost," it's hard to know where to start.
In that case, I'll say, it's theater that really works.
Ghost succeeds best when it remembers that it's supposed to be a musical, and that the relationships between the characters should drive the action rather than the reverse.
But the lyrics, co-written by Rubin and the composers, are more likely to make you laugh than cry.
Like Spider-Man Turn Off the Dark, the musical version of Ghost haunts the eye, not the ear.
Although the video projections are slick and impressive, they quickly become overwhelming, reducing the film's romantic intimacy into bloated and dizzying spectacle.
Warchus has turned a touching silver-screen love story into an overly flashy showbiz musical that betrays the intimacy of its source.
It’s a crying shame “Ghost” gets it so wrong.

Unsurprisingly, Rob Howell’s physical production (with video and projections by Jon Driscoll, illusions by Paul Kieve, lighting by Hugh Vanstone and sound by Bobby Aitken) vastly overwhelm the slim plot.

cn.t: Critics find "Ghost The Musical" a technically dazzling but emotionally hollow spectacle that relies heavily on special effects to compensate for forgettable songs, weak dialogue, and a story that never justifies its stage adaptation.
